paras: The lynching of Jim Rhodes took place in the early morning of October 2, 1882, when masked, armed men took him from the jail at Charlottesville, Virginia, and hanged him from an oak tree on the Free Bridge road. Rhodes was awaiting trial for the axe murders of John O. Massie and his wife, an elderly Albemarle County couple, and the lynchers held off the commonwealth's attorney at gunpoint. Virginia papers disputed whether his last words were a confession and whether the jail's guards had been overpowered.

The Massies were killed with an axe in their home about eight miles from Charlottesville on the night of March 7, 1882, and their house was robbed. Suspicion fell on Rhodes after his brother Leroy spent money freely in Charlottesville, and bloodstained clothing was reported found at the family's house in the Flat Woods. Rhodes fled to Tennessee, where a deputy sheriff arrested him in a Newport barroom on September 18 under the name William Allen.
According to the Staunton Vindicator, it was "well understood" in the county that he would be lynched once identified, together with his brother Lee.

A jail guard told the Richmond Dispatch that four men tried to enter the jail yard about 11 o'clock Sunday night and withdrew when the inner guard resisted. Between 1 and 2 a.m. a larger party forced the keys from jailer Wright, who refused to accompany them, saying, "You can riddle me with balls first." The men took Rhodes from his cell, where he fought them with his bed slats, but at Wright's entreaty they turned back from taking his brother upstairs.

The lynchers carried Rhodes about half a mile to an oak on Capt. T. L. Farish's farm, picketing the road at both ends. Commonwealth's Attorney Woods followed and demanded in the name of the Commonwealth that they desist, but armed men turned him and other citizens back with levelled guns. Rhodes was hanged, lowered when he begged for time, and hauled up again; most detailed accounts say he would only declare that his mother and brother were innocent.

After the lynchers dispersed, the town sergeant cut the body down on Woods's order, and an effort to revive Rhodes failed. Streams of people went out that morning to see the body, which, according to the Chronicle, hung until about 7 o'clock before it was brought to the jail.

A coroner's jury was summoned for an inquest on October 3, and a special grand jury was ordered to investigate the lynching. The lynchers were reported disguised and unrecognized, and no inquest verdict, arrest or indictment appears in the coverage. Leroy Rhodes was later tried in the circuit court at Charlottesville, convicted of second-degree murder in the Massie case and sentenced to eleven years.
On October 4 Col. C. C. Wertenbaker wrote to the Dispatch that the two sentries had been "neither overpowered or intimidated" and would have fired had their orders allowed it.

The Associated Press dispatch from Charlottesville ran on October 2 and 3 in papers from Washington and Savannah to St. Paul and Las Vegas, usually calling Rhodes "the murderer of the Massie family". Headlines such as "JUDGE LYNCH" and "A MURDERER SWUNG TO A LIMB" took his guilt for granted, and the Daily Gazette headed its first report "A FIEND'S JUST END".

Virginia papers printed longer accounts from the Charlottesville Chronicle and Jeffersonian extras and their own correspondents. The Dispatch's correspondent wrote that the community's disapproval scarcely expressed its "horror" while acknowledging an "assent" to a "just though fearful retribution", a passage the Valley Virginian reprinted. The Vindicator's correspondent quoted a prominent citizen who called the lynching "a blot on our county" in public while privately holding that "it was the right thing to do."

An early dispatch printed by the Daily Gazette said Rhodes acknowledged killing the couple, and some briefs repeated that he confessed, but the AP wire and the detailed Virginia accounts say he only identified himself and cleared his relatives.

The Daily Gazette and the Daily Republican called Rhodes "colored", while no Virginia account in the coverage stated his race and the Vindicator described his Flat Woods neighborhood as inhabited by "a class of whites".

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Rhodes
bases: Armed, masked men took Rhodes from the Charlottesville jail and hanged him to an oak tree while officials were held off at gunpoint (A13, A16, A17, A28).

A party of thirty to 150 armed men, by different counts, seized Rhodes from jail, where he awaited trial for the Massie murders, and hanged him against the commonwealth's attorney's demand that the law take its course (A10, A13, A16, A17, A28).

The AP wire, the Richmond Dispatch correspondent, the Charlottesville Chronicle and Jeffersonian extras and the Staunton Vindicator correspondent independently agree on the seizure and hanging (A5, A13, A16, A17, A33).

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch correspondent (jail guard)
accounts.gist: Four men failed at 11 p.m.; 35-40 men later forced the keys from the jailer, overpowered the outer guard and took Rhodes, who fought with bed slats.

accounts.label: Charlottesville Chronicle and Jeffersonian extras
accounts.gist: About 150 men, some 50 at the jail; jailer Wright gave up the keys only under threat; Woods stopped at a picket line; body hung till 7 a.m.

accounts.label: Staunton Vindicator correspondent
accounts.gist: 75 to 100 armed men came for both brothers but yielded to the jailer's entreaties and took only Jim; the lynching had been expected for days.

accounts.label: Guard commander
accounts.gist: Col. Wertenbaker wrote that the sentries were neither overpowered nor intimidated but obeyed orders not to fire.

framing.detail: The Daily Gazette headlined 'A FIEND'S JUST END' and later 'THE MURDER OF AN OLD COUPLE AVENGED'.
The Richmond Dispatch reported community 'horror' while allowing an 'assent' to a 'just though fearful retribution'.
The Vindicator called the Massie killing one of the most 'brutal tragedies' in Virginia and described the lynching in detail without endorsement.
Northern and western papers ran short wires under heads like 'JUDGE LYNCH' and 'A Murderer Lynched in Virginia'.

versions.value: Only identified himself and cleared his mother and brother; no confession of his own guilt

conflicts.note: The detailed Virginia reports, including the Dispatch's guard source, deny a confession; the confession claim appears in early brief wires.
